player.speaker: Revolutionary Delegate
line.reaction-briliant.speaker: Emil Barth
line.reaction-briliant.text: The delegates at Lehrter station were arguing over whether your column could possibly arrive intact. Then it marched off the train before they finished. Berlin is the last question, comrade, and for once we ask it from strength.
line.reaction-tactical.speaker: Emil Barth
line.reaction-tactical.text: Your column reached Berlin behind its own casualty lists. The Majority Socialists are reading those names when they speak of order and continuity, and frightened people will listen to them.
line.reaction-victory.speaker: Emil Barth
line.reaction-victory.text: They know your column in the working districts now. What they do not know is whether Berlin will turn the councils' movement into power—or into a negotiation conducted over their heads.
line.extra-workers-armed.speaker: Emil Barth
line.extra-workers-armed.text: Word that you armed the workers in Frankfurt reached Berlin yesterday. Our factory battalions are in the streets now; they did not wait to be asked. That is our strength—and exactly what the Majority Socialists point to when they call for order.
line.extra-alternate-history.speaker: Emil Barth
line.extra-alternate-history.text: Every city you crossed was meant to be isolated before the next one moved. Instead your trains carried delegates, rifles and confidence toward Berlin. The ministries assumed obedience would travel faster than revolt; this week proved the opposite.
line.callback-frankfurt-held.speaker: Emil Barth
line.callback-frankfurt-held.text: You left Frankfurt with its city, bridges and station under council guard. The Rhine-Main delegates arriving behind you carry mandates now, not petitions.
line.callback-frankfurt-lost.speaker: Emil Barth
line.callback-frankfurt-lost.text: You had to leave Frankfurt before its council closed its hand on the whole city. The government still has a functioning administration in the west, and it is using it against us.
line.callback-frankfurt-railways.speaker: Anna Keller
line.callback-frankfurt-railways.text: You told us to take the railway before the proclamations. We did. The government still has telephones, but the delegates arriving at Berlin carry our orders and our account of Frankfurt. Do not waste what we bought you.
line.berlin-awakens.speaker: Emil Barth
line.berlin-awakens.text: Listen—the factory whistles began before dawn and have not stopped. Columns are leaving Moabit, Wedding and the eastern works; soldiers at the gates argue over whether the Kaiser has already abdicated. Inside the ministries, clerks keep stamping imperial forms as if paper could hold the city together.
line.barth-opening.speaker: Emil Barth
line.barth-opening.text: The strike is walking toward us: factory hands, soldiers' delegates, prisoners just out of the cells. The ministries still hold the centre. Wait for them to admit they have lost Berlin, and Ebert will be inside before we are.
line.haase-counterargument.speaker: Hugo Haase
line.haase-counterargument.text: Karl, a republic proclaimed from the street can still starve in the street. Millions who want the Kaiser gone do not all want the councils to replace elections. If we make every clerk and returning soldier choose between Ebert and civil war today, fear will choose for them.
line.liebknecht-question.speaker: Karl Liebknecht
line.liebknecht-question.text: And a ministry can call elections while the old officers, judges and police remain at their desks. Ebert offers continuity because he fears chaos; I fear continuity because it can bury the revolution without restoring the Kaiser. Delegate, which danger does your column answer first?
line.liebknecht-question.choice.governme: Drive directly toward the Reichstag and government quarter. The revolution must visibly replace imperial authority.
Gain a prestige award and experience for every core formation, but forgo full resupply and the experienced sailor detachment.
line.liebknecht-question.choice.barracks: Secure the barracks, stations and telegraph offices first. No proclamation will survive if loyalist troops control Berlin's communications.
Fully resupply every core formation and gain an experienced sailor detachment, but forgo the government-quarter prestige and core-wide experience.
line.haase-government.speaker: Hugo Haase
line.haase-government.text: Then you have chosen Liebknecht's symbol over my caution. I will not obstruct the march, but symbols do not feed columns or keep soldiers together. Maintain contact with the workers' districts and barracks—or the government quarter will become a stage surrounded by someone else's troops.
line.barth-infrastructure.speaker: Emil Barth
line.barth-infrastructure.text: Then the stations and telegraph offices must fall in the first hours. Stop military trains, seize government messages, and make every captured barracks elect delegates. We need obedience to pass from the officers to the councils, not merely buildings to change hands.
line.liebknecht-infrastructure-objection: Necessary—and politically timid. Every hour spent securing a signal box is an hour in which the Majority Socialists speak for the revolution from imperial offices. Win your barracks, Delegate. Then decide whether you have preserved the councils' power or merely made Ebert's republic safe.
line.ebert-dispatch.speaker: SPD Headquarters
line.ebert-dispatch.text: Political dispatch from SPD headquarters: Friedrich Ebert calls for order, food distribution, an armistice government and elections. He warns that civil war will destroy the republic before it is born. The ministries are preparing to survive the fall of the Kaiser.
line.liebknecht-final.speaker: Karl Liebknecht
line.liebknecht-final.text: Then enter the centre as an organised force, not a crowd waiting for permission. Break the last armed resistance, open the prisons and government quarter, and make certain that when the monarchy falls, power does not simply pass from a uniform to a ministerial desk.
epilogue.government-quarter-victory.text: Your council columns reached the political centre before the imperial offices could change their signs. The Kaiser is gone. Haase is already asking who will issue tomorrow's orders—and which councils will still be obeyed.
epilogue.government-quarter-defeat.text: The march fixed every loyal gun on the government quarter. Survivors came back without the centre and without much of the force that tried to take it. They will remember the courage; I will remember what it cost.
epilogue.military-infrastructure-victory: No loyal train entered Berlin, and the barracks elected delegates. While you secured them, Ebert entered the ministries. The Kaiser is gone, Delegate. The old desks have new occupants and our guards outside their doors.
We held platforms, messages and armouries until each became an island. The old command took them back one at a time. Some comrades escaped because of your caution. None of those buildings became power.
